Homework 7

Modes of convergence (LLN, CLT, √n) and Bayesian inference

Contents: Part 1 — Modes of convergence, LLN, CLT and the √n law · Part 2 — Conditional probability, Bayes’ theorem and Bayesian inference. Every number below comes from the script at the end of the page (seed 2026).

Part 1 — Modes of convergence in probability theory

1. The four modes

Let X₁, X₂, … and X be random variables. A sequence of numbers has one notion of limit; a sequence of functions on a probability space has several, because “Xₙ is close to X” can be measured pointwise, in probability, in average, or only through the laws.

modenotationdefinitionwhat has to be small
almost sure (a.s.)Xₙ → X a.s.P( limn→∞ Xₙ = X ) = 1the whole tail supk≥n|Xk − X| for a single outcome ω
in probabilityXₙ →P X∀ε>0: P(|Xₙ − X| > ε) → 0the probability of a large deviation at each fixed n
mean square (L²)Xₙ →L² XE[(Xₙ − X)²] → 0the average squared distance (needs finite second moments)
in distributionXₙ ⇒ XFₙ(x) → F(x) at every continuity point x of Fonly the laws: Xₙ and X need not live on the same probability space

Relations

a.s. ⇒ in probability ⇒ in distribution ; Lp ⇒ Lq (p > q ≥ 1) ⇒ in probability

No arrow can be reversed in general (examples below). Two partial converses are important: (i) if Xₙ ⇒ c with c a constant, then Xₙ →P c; (ii) if Xₙ → X in probability then some subsequence converges a.s.; and if |Xₙ| is dominated by an integrable variable (or is uniformly integrable) convergence in probability upgrades to convergence in L¹. Convergence in distribution can be turned into a.s. convergence on a new probability space (Skorokhod representation), which is how many proofs use it.

Why the converses fail

sequencea.s.in prob.L²comment
Typewriter: Xₙ = 1 on the n-th interval of the sweep [0,1], [0,½],[½,1], [0,⅓],…noyesyesP(Xₙ=1) = 1/m(n) → 0, E Xₙ² = 1/m(n) → 0, but every ω is hit once per sweep, so Xₙ(ω)=1 infinitely often (e.g. ω = 0.5 is hit 67 times in the first 1035 terms)
Xₙ = n·1[0,1/n](U), U ~ Uniform(0,1)yesyesnofor fixed ω Xₙ(ω) = 0 once n > 1/ω; but E Xₙ = 1 and E Xₙ² = n (no mass is “lost” in probability, but it escapes in the mean)
Xₙ = (−1)ⁿ Z, Z ~ N(0,1)nononoevery Xₙ ~ N(0,1), so Xₙ ⇒ Z; yet for odd n, P(|Xₙ − Z| > 1) = P(|2Z| > 1) = 0.617 for all odd n
X̄ₙ of iid standard Cauchynononono mean exists; X̄ₙ is again standard Cauchy for every n (check: n = 1000, 4000 replications, KS distance to Cauchy 0.0087, p = 0.92); it converges in law (trivially) but not in any stronger sense

Intuition. a.s. convergence is a statement about one infinite run: after some (random) N the sequence stays near the limit forever. Convergence in probability only says that at each fixed large n the chance of being far away is small — the far-away events can still happen infinitely often, but ever more rarely (typewriter). L² controls the average and therefore also the rare-but-huge excursions, which in probability ignores (case (c)). Convergence in distribution forgets which outcome produced which value.

2. Roles in the LLN, the CLT and elsewhere in statistics

resultstatementmodekey assumptions
Weak LLN (Khinchin)Xn → μin probabilityiid, E|X| < ∞. With a finite variance, Chebyshev gives it in one line
Strong LLN (Kolmogorov)Xn → μalmost surelyiid, E|X| < ∞ (and this is also necessary)
Variance lawE(Xn − μ)² = σ²/nmean squareuncorrelated, common variance σ²; exact for every n
CLT (Lindeberg–Lévy)√n(Xn − μ)/σ ⇒ N(0,1)in distributioniid, 0 < σ² < ∞ (Lindeberg–Feller: independent, not identically distributed)
Slutsky + consistency of st-statistic √n(X̄ₙ − μ)/s ⇒ N(0,1)in probability (s→σ) combined with in distributions² →P σ², then Slutsky’s lemma
Delta method√n(g(X̄ₙ) − g(μ)) ⇒ N(0, g′(μ)²σ²)in distributiong differentiable at μ, g′(μ) ≠ 0
Consistency of estimatorsθ̂ₙ → θin probability (weak) or a.s. (strong)e.g. the MLE under regularity conditions
Asymptotic normality of the MLE√n(θ̂ₙ − θ) ⇒ N(0, I(θ)⁻¹)in distributionregular model, I(θ) Fisher information
Glivenko–Cantellisupx|F̂ₙ(x) − F(x)| → 0almost surelyiid sample, any F
  • LLN. The weak law is convergence in probability: for every ε, P(|Xn − μ| > ε) ≤ σ²/(nε²) (Chebyshev), which is also exactly convergence in L². The strong law is the stronger a.s. statement: the single sequence of averages one will actually observe converges, as in panel (a) above. For statistics, consistency of an estimator is a weak LLN-type statement, and a.s. consistency is the strong one.
  • CLT. The natural mode is convergence in distribution, because the normalised average Zₙ = √n(Xn − μ)/σ has a non-degenerate limit: it keeps fluctuating and does not converge to any random variable in probability or a.s. (the law of the iterated logarithm says limsup Zₙ/√(2 log log n) = 1 a.s.). What converges is the distribution of Zₙ: Fₙ(z) → Φ(z).
  • How fast? For Exp(1) data the distribution of Zₙ is known exactly (X̄ₙ ~ Gamma(n, 1/n)), so the Kolmogorov distance sup|Fₙ − Φ| can be computed without Monte Carlo. Its fitted log-log slope is -0.50, i.e. O(n−1/2) as the Berry–Esseen theorem predicts; at n = 215 it equals 0.00907, matching the first Edgeworth term skewness·φ(0)/(6√n) = 0.00907. The sample skewness of Zₙ falls like 2/√n:
n12530200
sample skewness of √n(X̄ₙ−μ)/σ1.991.410.910.370.14
theory 2/√n2.001.410.890.370.14
  • Combining modes (Slutsky). The workhorse t-statistic mixes two modes: s →P σ (a LLN-type fact) and √n(Xn − μ)/σ ⇒ N(0,1) (CLT) together give √n(Xn − μ)/s ⇒ N(0,1). The delta method and the asymptotic normality of the MLE are likewise “CLT + continuous mapping/Slutsky”, so they inherit convergence in distribution.

3. Why √n?

Additivity of variance

For Sₙ = X₁ + … + Xₙ with common variance σ²:

Var(Sₙ) = Σᵢ Var(Xᵢ) + 2 Σi<j Cov(Xᵢ, Xⱼ) = nσ² if the Xᵢ are independent (or merely uncorrelated)

so sd(Sₙ) = σ√n grows like √n — much more slowly than the n of the mean, nμ — and sd(Xn) = σ/√n. Hence the exact identity E(Xn − μ)² = σ²/n of panel (d) below (L² convergence at rate 1/n in squared units, 1/√n in the units of X). The fluctuations of Sₙ − nμ live on the scale √n, so √n is the unique normalisation that gives a limit that is neither 0 nor ∞:

sd( nᵃ (Xn − μ) ) = σ · na − 1/2 → 0 (a < ½), σ (a = ½), ∞ (a > ½)

The role of independence

The √n law is a statement about the cross terms. They vanish for independent (or uncorrelated) variables. Otherwise:

  • Short-range dependence (e.g. a stationary AR(1) with autocorrelation φ): n·Var(Xn) → σ²(1 + φ)/(1 − φ) = γ(0) + 2Σₖ γ(k). The √n scale survives, but the effective variance changes: with φ = 0.7 it is 5.67 times σ² (simulated 5.87 at n = 2000). Treating dependent data as independent understates the standard error by a factor √5.67 ≈ 2.4 here.
  • Common-factor dependence (equicorrelation ρ): Var(Xn) = ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ²/n does not go to 0. The average converges, but to the common factor and not to μ: there is no LLN to μ, and n·Var grows linearly (red curve).
  • Heavy tails. If Var = ∞ the argument breaks. For the Cauchy law the mean of n observations has the same law as one observation, so averaging does not help at all (panel (d) of the first figure); in general, for stable laws of index α < 2 the right scale is n1/α, not √n.
n103010030010002000
independent N(0,1)0.991.010.971.021.011.01
AR(1), φ = 0.7 (limit 5.67)4.115.105.585.925.885.87
equicorrelated, ρ = 0.3 (theory ρn + 1 − ρ)3.8 (3.7)9.9 (9.7)31.2 (30.7)91.8 (90.7)305.1 (300.7)608.8 (600.7)

Entries: n·Var(Xn) from 4000 simulated series of unit variance.

Consequences in statistical inference

  • Standard error σ/√n: to halve the error you need 4 times the data; one more correct decimal costs 100 times the data (e.g. Monte Carlo error 1/√N).
  • Confidence intervals and tests: Xn ± z·s/√n and the statistic √n(Xn − μ₀)/s are built on exactly this scaling.
  • Estimators: “√n-consistent” and asymptotically normal estimators (MLE, M-estimators, via the delta method) have standard errors of order 1/√n; the asymptotic variance, I(θ)⁻¹ for the MLE, is the price of dependence and model structure in the constant, not in the rate.
  • Warning. All of this relies on independence (or a controlled dependence structure) and finite variance; checking those is part of the inference, not a formality.

Part 2 — Conditional probability, Bayes’ theorem and statistical inference

4. Conditional probability

For events with P(B) > 0: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B), the probability of A when the sample space is restricted to B. Immediate consequences: the multiplication rule P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B)P(B); the law of total probability P(A) = Σᵢ P(A | Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ) for a partition {Bᵢ}; and the characterisation of independence: A, B independent ⇔ P(A | B) = P(A). For random variables with densities, f(y | x) = f(x, y)/f(x).

In probability theory the model is fixed and we ask about data: P(data | model). In statistics the model parameter θ is unknown and we want to say something about it from data; the two conditional probabilities go in opposite directions and are not equal: P(data | θ) ≠ P(θ | data). Confusing them is the “prosecutor’s fallacy”; Bayes’ theorem is the exact bridge.

5. Bayes’ theorem and its three ingredients

Events: P(B | A) = P(A | B) P(B) / P(A), with P(A) = Σ P(A | Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ). Odds form: posterior odds = likelihood ratio × prior odds. Parameters and data:

π(θ | x) = L(θ; x) π(θ) / m(x) , m(x) = ∫ L(θ; x) π(θ) dθ ⇒ posterior ∝ likelihood × prior
  • Prior π(θ): what is believed about θ before seeing the data (previous studies, physical constraints, expert knowledge, or a deliberately vague choice).
  • Likelihood L(θ; x) = f(x | θ): the probability (density) of the observed data, viewed as a function of θ. It is not a probability distribution over θ (it need not integrate to 1) and it carries all the information of the data about θ in the model (likelihood principle).
  • Posterior π(θ | x): the updated distribution of θ after seeing x. The normalising constant m(x) (marginal likelihood or evidence) does not depend on θ; it matters for model comparison (Bayes factors) and, when no closed form exists, is the reason why computation (MCMC, variational methods) is needed.

Why updating is central. (i) It answers the question one actually has, “how plausible is each θ given what I saw?”, and returns a full distribution: point estimates (posterior mean, MAP), credible intervals, probabilities of hypotheses and predictions all follow. (ii) It is sequential: today’s posterior is tomorrow’s prior, and for conditionally independent data the result is the same whether data arrive one batch at a time or all at once (checked numerically below). (iii) Predictions integrate over the parameter uncertainty (posterior predictive). (iv) With enough data the prior’s influence fades (Bernstein–von Mises: the posterior is approximately N(θ̂, I(θ̂)⁻¹/n) for a prior with positive density at the truth), linking Bayesian and likelihood-based inference through the CLT of Part 1.

6. Example 1 — a base-rate problem: an intrusion detector

An IDS flags an event as an attack with probability 0.99 if it is an attack (sensitivity, TPR) and 0.01 if it is benign (false-positive rate). Suppose one event in 10 000 is an attack (prior 10⁻⁴). The likelihood of the observation “alert” is 0.99 under “attack” and 0.01 under “benign”. Bayes:

P(attack | alert) = 0.99·10⁻⁴ / (0.99·10⁻⁴ + 0.01·(1 − 10⁻⁴)) = 0.0098 ≈ 1%

In natural frequencies: of 1 000 000 events, 100 are attacks and 99 are detected, but 9999 benign events also trigger an alert, so only about 1 alert in 102 is real. This is the base-rate fallacy for intrusion detection (discussed by Axelsson, 2000), and it happens although the detector “is 99% accurate”: the posterior is dominated by the prior. The test is very informative the other way: P(attack | no alert) is about 1.0e-06.

among 1 000 000 eventsalertno alerttotal
attack (prior 10⁻⁴)991100
benign9999989901999900
total100989899021 000 000

Updating. If a second, conditionally independent sensor with the same characteristics also raises an alert, the posterior of the first step becomes the new prior: the odds are multiplied by the likelihood ratio 99 again, giving P(attack | two alerts) = 0.495 (from 0.0098). This assumes the two sensors are conditionally independent given the true state; correlated sensors would give much less.

Lessons. The prior (base rate) matters as much as the likelihood; improving the false-positive rate by a factor 10 or 100 helps far more than improving the sensitivity from 0.99 to 0.999.

7. Example 2 — estimating a proportion (Beta–Binomial)

Data: k successes in n trials, L(p) ∝ pk(1−p)n−k. With a Beta(a, b) prior the posterior is again a Beta (conjugacy), and the update is simple counting:

p | k ~ Beta(a + k, b + n − k) , E[p | k] = (a + k)/(a + b + n) = w·(k/n) + (1 − w)·a/(a + b) , w = n/(a + b + n)

The prior acts like a + b pseudo-observations, and the posterior mean is a weighted average of the data proportion and the prior mean, with weight on the data n/(a + b + n) → 1. Four priors are compared: uniform Beta(1,1), Jeffreys Beta(½,½), a strong prior centred at ½ (Beta(50,50)), and a deliberately misleading one centred near 0.09 (Beta(2,20)). The data have the same proportion 0.7 at three sample sizes.

n = 1000, k = 700MLE 0.70; Clopper–Pearson [0.671, 0.728]0.700 [0.671, 0.728] (weight on data 1.00)0.700 [0.671, 0.728] (weight on data 1.00)0.682 [0.654, 0.709] (weight on data 0.91)0.687 [0.658, 0.715] (weight on data 0.98)
  • n = 10: the conclusion depends on the prior. With Beta(2,20) the posterior mean is 0.28 and the 95% credible interval [0.14, 0.45] excludes the sample proportion 0.7 altogether; the strong prior pulls the mean to 0.52.
  • n = 100: the priors still disagree visibly (misleading prior: [0.502, 0.676], which still excludes 0.7).
  • n = 1000: all four intervals nearly coincide and the posterior is essentially the normalised likelihood (the uniform-prior posterior, Beta(k+1, n−k+1), is exactly that): the data have overwhelmed the prior.

Sequential updating check. Starting from Beta(2,20) and updating with four batches (successes/trials = 3/5, 9/15, 20/30, 38/55) gives Beta(72, 55), identical to a single update with all 105 trials and 70 successes (asserted in the code).

8. Example 3 — attack counts per day (Poisson–Gamma) and prediction

Daily numbers of attacks on a server are modelled as Poisson(λ). A Gamma(a, b) prior (shape a, rate b) gives the posterior Gamma(a + Σxᵢ, b + n), and the posterior predictive for the next day is negative binomial. Simulated data (true λ = 4, unknown to the analyst): [2, 4, 3, 5, 4, 5, 2, 3, 4, 3], sum 35, n = 10, maximum-likelihood estimate λ̂ = 3.5. Three priors: vague Gamma(1, 0.1) (mean 10, sd 10), informative and correct Gamma(8, 2) (mean 4), misleading Gamma(30, 2) (mean 15).

priorprior meanposterior mean95% credible interval for λP(next day ≥ 10 attacks)
Vague Gamma(1, 0.1)10.03.56[2.50, 4.82]0.59%
Informative Gamma(8, 2)4.03.58[2.59, 4.73]0.57%
Misleading Gamma(30, 2)15.05.42[4.18, 6.81]5.67%
plug-in Poisson(λ̂ = 3.5)—3.50—0.33%
  • The vague and the informative priors agree closely after 10 days (posterior means 3.56 and 3.58); the informative one gives a slightly narrower interval, i.e. a small gain from correct prior information.
  • The misleading prior moves the posterior mean to 5.42, with a 95% interval [4.18, 6.81] that does not contain the true λ = 4: a confidently wrong conclusion that would only fade with more data.
  • Prediction. The probability of a day with at least 10 attacks is 0.59% under the vague posterior predictive but 0.33% with the plug-in Poisson(λ̂): plugging in the point estimate ignores the uncertainty about λ and understates the tail risk. With the misleading prior it is 5.67%.

9. How priors and likelihoods shape the conclusions: advantages and limitations

A prior is not neutral, but its effect can be measured. For n = 20 trials I computed exactly (summing the binomial probabilities, no simulation) how often each 95% interval contains the true p — its frequentist coverage:

interval (n = 20)mean coverage, p ∈ [0.05, 0.95]minimum coveragecoverage at p = 0.7coverage at p = 0.1
Uniform Beta(1,1)95.4%91.0%97.5%95.7%
Jeffreys Beta(½,½)94.9%89.5%94.7%95.7%
Misleading Beta(2,20)32.8%0.0%0.0%99.8%
Wald (frequentist)89.8%63.9%94.7%87.6%
Clopper–Pearson97.6%95.8%97.5%98.9%
  • With a vague prior (uniform or Jeffreys) the Bayesian credible intervals have good coverage (mean 95.4% and 94.9%), better than the Wald interval (mean 89.8%, minimum 63.9%), and close to the conservative Clopper–Pearson interval.
  • With the misleading Beta(2,20) prior the mean coverage drops to 32.8% and is 0.0% at p = 0.7; it over-covers near the prior’s own centre (p = 0.1: 99.8%). A credible interval is guaranteed to be right only on average over the prior.

Advantages

  • Direct probability statements about parameters and hypotheses (“P(λ > 5 | data) = …”), with a full posterior and predictive distribution.
  • Honest treatment of small samples and the possibility to include genuine prior information (previous studies, base rates); sequential and hierarchical modelling.
  • Uncertainty propagates automatically into predictions and decisions (Example 3).

Limitations

  • Subjectivity and sensitivity. Different priors give different answers when data are scarce (Example 2, n = 10). Good practice: report a sensitivity analysis with several priors, and prefer weakly informative priors when no real knowledge exists. “Uninformative” priors are not always uniform: they change with the parametrisation.
  • Zero prior probability is final. If π(θ) = 0 then π(θ | x) = 0 whatever the data (Cromwell’s rule: avoid probabilities 0 and 1 for things that are not logically impossible). Improper priors can give improper posteriors.
  • The likelihood is a model. The posterior is only as good as the model for the data: wrong independence assumptions (two “independent” sensors that are not, Part 1’s dependence examples) or wrong distributions are not repaired by Bayes’ theorem.
  • Computation. Outside conjugate families the evidence m(x) has no closed form and needs numerical integration or MCMC.
  • Interpretation. A 95% credible interval means P(θ in interval | data) = 0.95 given the prior and model; a 95% confidence interval is a statement about the procedure over repeated samples. The two coincide approximately only when the prior is vague and n is large (Bernstein–von Mises).

10. Conclusions

  • The modes of convergence are ordered a.s. ⇒ in probability ⇒ in distribution and L² ⇒ in probability, with counterexamples for every reverse implication. The LLN needs convergence of the average to a constant (in probability or a.s.), the CLT only convergence of laws.
  • √n comes from Var(ΣXᵢ) = nσ² under independence or uncorrelation; with dependence the constant (or even the rate) changes, with infinite variance the scale is not √n.
  • Bayes’ theorem turns the probability of the data given the parameter into the probability of the parameter given the data; the prior matters most when data are few or the event is rare, and fades as n grows.

Limitations: simulations use one seed; the Exp(1), Bernoulli, Poisson and Cauchy cases are illustrations, not proofs; the IDS numbers are hypothetical, not measured rates.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Homework 7 - Part 1: modes of convergence, LLN, CLT and the sqrt(n) law  (simulations)
             Part 2: conditional probability, Bayes' theorem, prior/likelihood/posterior (examples)
Run: python3 hw8_convergence_bayes.py   -> figures + results4.json in ../build
"""
import json, math, os
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)); BUILD = os.path.join(HERE, "..", "build")
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
R = {}

BG, TXT, MUTED, GRID = "#171e2e", "#e6eaf2", "#8d98b0", "#2a3550"
COL = ["#4da3ff", "#6ee7a8", "#e86f8c", "#f2a65a", "#c4a7ff", "#f5e663"]
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.facecolor": BG, "axes.facecolor": BG, "savefig.facecolor": BG, "text.color": TXT,
    "axes.labelcolor": TXT, "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "axes.edgecolor": GRID, "grid.color": GRID,
    "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": .7, "font.size": 10, "axes.titlesize": 11, "legend.facecolor": BG, "legend.edgecolor": GRID})
def save(fig, name): fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(os.path.join(BUILD, name), dpi=140); plt.close(fig)

# =============================================================== PART 1
# ---- 1a modes of convergence: four panels
fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 7.6))
# (a) a.s. convergence of running means (Exp(1))
N = 5000; ns = np.arange(1, N + 1)
ax = axs[0, 0]
for _ in range(25):
    ax.plot(ns, np.cumsum(rng.exponential(1, N)) / ns, lw=.8, alpha=.8, color=COL[0])
ax.plot(ns, 1 + 3 / np.sqrt(ns), "--", color=COL[3], lw=1.2, label="μ ± 3σ/√n"); ax.plot(ns, 1 - 3 / np.sqrt(ns), "--", color=COL[3], lw=1.2)
ax.axhline(1, color=TXT, lw=.8); ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_ylim(.2, 3)
ax.set_title("(a) 25 sample paths of the running mean, Exp(1): each path → μ = 1"); ax.set_xlabel("n"); ax.legend()
# (b) typewriter sequence: in probability / L^p, not a.s.
Mst = 45; seq = []                      # stage m: intervals [(j-1)/m, j/m], j = 1..m
for m in range(1, Mst + 1):
    for j in range(1, m + 1): seq.append((m, (j - 1) / m, j / m))
nn = len(seq); pr = np.array([1 / s[0] for s in seq])
ax = axs[0, 1]; ax.step(np.arange(1, nn + 1), pr, color=COL[1], where="post", label="P(Xₙ = 1) = 1/m(n) → 0")
for k, om in enumerate([0.137, 0.5, 0.9]):
    hits = [i + 1 for i, s in enumerate(seq) if s[1] <= om <= s[2]]
    ax.plot(hits, [-.08 - .1 * k] * len(hits), "|", color=COL[[0, 2, 3][k]], ms=10, label=f"n with Xₙ(ω)=1, ω={om}")
R["typewriter"] = {"n_terms": nn, "hits_per_omega": {str(om): sum(1 for s in seq if s[1] <= om <= s[2]) for om in (0.137, 0.5, 0.9)}}
ax.set_ylim(-.45, 1.05); ax.set_title("(b) “typewriter” sequence: Xₙ → 0 in probability and in L², but not a.s."); ax.set_xlabel("n"); ax.legend(loc="center right", fontsize=8)
# (c) n * 1_[0,1/n]: a.s. and in probability, not in L^1 / L^2
nv = np.unique(np.logspace(0, 4, 40).astype(int)); ax = axs[1, 0]
ax.loglog(nv, 1 / nv, color=COL[1], label="P(Xₙ ≠ 0) = 1/n → 0"); ax.loglog(nv, np.ones_like(nv), color=COL[0], label="E|Xₙ| = 1 (does not → 0)")
ax.loglog(nv, nv.astype(float), color=COL[2], label="E Xₙ² = n → ∞")
ax.set_title("(c) Xₙ = n·1[0,1/n](U): →0 a.s. and in probability, but not in L¹ or L²"); ax.set_xlabel("n"); ax.legend()
# (d) Cauchy running mean does not converge (no mean => LLN fails)
N2 = 20000; n2 = np.arange(1, N2 + 1); ax = axs[1, 1]
for _ in range(8): ax.plot(n2, np.cumsum(rng.standard_cauchy(N2)) / n2, lw=.8, color=COL[2], alpha=.9)
ax.plot(n2, np.cumsum(rng.standard_normal(N2)) / n2, lw=1.4, color=COL[1], label="N(0,1) running mean (converges)")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_ylim(-8, 8); ax.set_title("(d) Cauchy running means (red) never settle: X̄ₙ ~ Cauchy for every n"); ax.set_xlabel("n"); ax.legend()
save(fig, "hw8_modes.png")
# check: mean of n Cauchy is again standard Cauchy -> KS vs Cauchy at n = 1000
cm = np.array([rng.standard_cauchy(1000).mean() for _ in range(4000)])
R["cauchy_mean_ks"] = float(stats.kstest(cm, "cauchy").statistic)
R["cauchy_mean_ks_pvalue"] = float(stats.kstest(cm, "cauchy").pvalue)

# ---- 1b CLT for Exp(1): exact via Gamma
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(15, 3.3), sharey=True)
zz = np.linspace(-4, 4, 400); R["clt_sample"] = {}
for ax, n in zip(axs, [1, 2, 5, 30, 200]):
    z = (rng.gamma(n, 1, 200000) / n - 1) * math.sqrt(n)
    ax.hist(z, bins=80, range=(-4, 4), density=True, color=COL[0], alpha=.7); ax.plot(zz, stats.norm.pdf(zz), color=COL[3], lw=1.5)
    ax.set_title(f"n = {n}"); ax.set_xlabel("√n (X̄ₙ − μ)/σ")
    R["clt_sample"][n] = {"skew": float(stats.skew(z)), "std": float(z.std())}
axs[0].set_ylabel("density"); save(fig, "hw8_clt.png")

# ---- 1c rates: KS distance (exact), scaling exponents, dependence, L2 rate
fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 8))
nlist = np.unique(np.logspace(0, 4, 25).astype(int)); zg = np.linspace(-8, 8, 40001); ks = []
for n in nlist:
    Fn = stats.gamma.cdf(n + zg * math.sqrt(n), a=n)
    ks.append(np.max(np.abs(Fn - stats.norm.cdf(zg))))
ks = np.array(ks); sl = np.polyfit(np.log(nlist[nlist >= 10]), np.log(ks[nlist >= 10]), 1)[0]
edge = 2 * stats.norm.pdf(0) / (6 * np.sqrt(nlist))      # Edgeworth first term: |skew| φ(0)/(6√n), skew = 2
R["ks"] = {"n": nlist.tolist(), "ks": ks.tolist(), "slope": float(sl), "edgeworth_at_200": float(edge[np.argmin(abs(nlist - 200))]),
           "ks_at_200": float(ks[np.argmin(abs(nlist - 200))]), "n200": int(nlist[np.argmin(abs(nlist - 200))])}
ax = axs[0, 0]; ax.loglog(nlist, ks, "o-", color=COL[0], label="sup |Fₙ − Φ|  (exact, Exp(1))"); ax.loglog(nlist, edge, "--", color=COL[3], label="skew·φ(0)/(6√n)")
ax.set_title(f"(a) CLT error decays like n^−1/2 (fitted slope {sl:.2f})"); ax.set_xlabel("n"); ax.legend()
# scaling exponent
ax = axs[0, 1]; nl = np.unique(np.logspace(1, 4, 14).astype(int)); R["scal"] = {}
for a, c in zip((0.3, 0.5, 0.7), COL):
    sd = [np.std(n ** a * (rng.gamma(n, 1, 20000) / n - 1)) for n in nl]; R["scal"][str(a)] = sd
    ax.loglog(nl, sd, "o-", color=c, label=f"sd of n^{a}(X̄ₙ − μ)")
ax.set_title("(b) only the exponent ½ gives a non-degenerate limit"); ax.set_xlabel("n"); ax.legend()
# dependence: n Var(Xbar)
nd = np.array([10, 30, 100, 300, 1000, 2000]); reps = 4000; phi_ = 0.7; rho = 0.3
v_iid, v_ar, v_eq = [], [], []
Z = rng.standard_normal((reps, nd.max()))
# stationary AR(1) with unit variance: x_t = phi x_{t-1} + sqrt(1-phi^2) z_t, x_0 ~ N(0,1)
x0 = rng.standard_normal((reps, 1)); ar = np.empty_like(Z); ar[:, 0:1] = x0
for t in range(1, nd.max()): ar[:, t] = phi_ * ar[:, t - 1] + math.sqrt(1 - phi_ ** 2) * Z[:, t]
W = rng.standard_normal((reps, 1)); eq = math.sqrt(rho) * W + math.sqrt(1 - rho) * rng.standard_normal((reps, nd.max()))
iid = rng.standard_normal((reps, nd.max()))
for n in nd:
    v_iid.append(n * iid[:, :n].mean(1).var()); v_ar.append(n * ar[:, :n].mean(1).var()); v_eq.append(n * eq[:, :n].mean(1).var())
lr = (1 + phi_) / (1 - phi_)
R["dep"] = {"n": nd.tolist(), "iid": v_iid, "ar": v_ar, "eq": v_eq, "lr_ar": lr, "eq_theory": [rho * n + (1 - rho) for n in nd.tolist()]}
ax = axs[1, 0]
ax.semilogx(nd, v_iid, "o-", color=COL[1], label="independent: n·Var(X̄ₙ) → σ² = 1")
ax.semilogx(nd, v_ar, "o-", color=COL[0], label=f"AR(1), φ={phi_}: → σ²(1+φ)/(1−φ) = {lr:.2f}"); ax.axhline(lr, color=COL[0], ls=":", lw=1)
ax.semilogx(nd, v_eq, "o-", color=COL[2], label=f"equicorrelated ρ={rho}: n·Var ≈ ρn → ∞")
ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_title("(c) dependence changes the constant — or destroys the √n law"); ax.set_xlabel("n"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
# L2 rate
ax = axs[1, 1]; nl2 = np.unique(np.logspace(0, 3.5, 20).astype(int)); R["l2"] = {}
for name, draw, s2, c in (("Exp(1), σ²=1", lambda n, r: rng.gamma(n, 1, r) / n - 1, 1.0, COL[0]),
                          ("Bernoulli(0.3), σ²=0.21", lambda n, r: rng.binomial(n, .3, r) / n - .3, .21, COL[1])):
    mse = [np.mean(draw(n, 40000) ** 2) for n in nl2]; R["l2"][name] = {"n": nl2.tolist(), "mse": mse}
    ax.loglog(nl2, mse, "o", color=c, label=f"MSE of X̄ₙ, {name}"); ax.loglog(nl2, s2 / nl2, "-", color=c, lw=1)
ax.set_title("(d) mean-square convergence: E(X̄ₙ − μ)² = σ²/n"); ax.set_xlabel("n"); ax.legend()
save(fig, "hw8_rates.png")
R["conv_dist_not_prob"] = float(2 * stats.norm.sf(.5))      # P(|(-Z) - Z| > 1) = P(|2Z|>1)

# =============================================================== PART 2
# ---- 2a base-rate fallacy (intrusion detection)
def post(prior, tpr, fpr): return prior * tpr / (prior * tpr + (1 - prior) * fpr)
ids = {"prior": 1e-4, "tpr": .99, "fpr": .01}
ids["ppv"] = post(**ids)
n_ev = 1_000_000; att = ids["prior"] * n_ev
ids["nat"] = {"attacks": att, "detected": att * ids["tpr"], "benign": n_ev - att, "false_alarms": (n_ev - att) * ids["fpr"]}
odds = ids["prior"] / (1 - ids["prior"]) * (ids["tpr"] / ids["fpr"]) ** 2
ids["two_alerts"] = odds / (1 + odds)
ids["npv"] = (1 - ids["prior"]) * (1 - ids["fpr"]) / ((1 - ids["prior"]) * (1 - ids["fpr"]) + ids["prior"] * (1 - ids["tpr"]))
R["ids"] = ids
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.6, 4.4)); pv = np.logspace(-6, -0.3, 300)
for fpr, c in ((.01, COL[2]), (.001, COL[3]), (.0001, COL[1])):
    ax.semilogx(pv, post(pv, .99, fpr), color=c, label=f"TPR 0.99, FPR {fpr:g}")
ax.plot([ids["prior"]], [ids["ppv"]], "o", color=TXT); ax.annotate(f"prior 10⁻⁴ → posterior {ids['ppv']:.3f}", (ids["prior"], ids["ppv"]), xytext=(2e-6, .45), color=TXT, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=MUTED))
ax.set_xlabel("prior probability that an event is an attack (base rate)"); ax.set_ylabel("P(attack | alert)"); ax.legend(); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.02)
save(fig, "hw8_ids.png")

# ---- 2b Beta-Binomial
priors = {"Uniform Beta(1,1)": (1, 1), "Jeffreys Beta(½,½)": (.5, .5), "Strong, centred Beta(50,50)": (50, 50), "Misleading Beta(2,20)": (2, 20)}
datasets = [(10, 7), (100, 70), (1000, 700)]
bb = []
for n, k in datasets:
    row = {"n": n, "k": k, "mle": k / n, "cp": [stats.beta.ppf(.025, k, n - k + 1) if k > 0 else 0.0, stats.beta.ppf(.975, k + 1, n - k) if k < n else 1.0], "post": {}}
    for name, (a, b) in priors.items():
        lo, hi = stats.beta.ppf([.025, .975], a + k, b + n - k)
        row["post"][name] = {"mean": (a + k) / (a + b + n), "lo": lo, "hi": hi, "w_data": n / (a + b + n), "map": ((a + k - 1) / (a + b + n - 2)) if a + k > 1 and b + n - k > 1 else None}
    bb.append(row)
R["bb"] = bb
# sequential updating = batch updating
a, b = 2, 20; ks_ = [3, 9, 20, 38]; ns_ = [5, 15, 30, 55]
sa, sb = a, b
for k_, n_ in zip(ks_, ns_): sa += k_; sb += n_ - k_
assert (sa, sb) == (a + sum(ks_), b + sum(ns_) - sum(ks_))
R["seq"] = {"final": [sa, sb], "total_n": sum(ns_), "total_k": sum(ks_)}
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(16, 3.8), sharex=True); p = np.linspace(0.001, .999, 600)
ax = axs[0]
for (name, (a, b)), c in zip(priors.items(), COL): ax.plot(p, stats.beta.pdf(p, a, b), color=c, label=name)
ax.set_title("priors"); ax.set_ylim(0, 8); ax.set_xlabel("p"); ax.legend(fontsize=7)
for ax, (n, k) in zip(axs[1:], datasets):
    for (name, (a, b)), c in zip(priors.items(), COL): ax.plot(p, stats.beta.pdf(p, a + k, b + n - k), color=c)
    ax.axvline(k / n, color=TXT, ls=":", lw=1); ax.set_title(f"posteriors, n = {n}, k = {k}"); ax.set_xlabel("p")
save(fig, "hw8_beta.png")

# ---- 2c Poisson-Gamma
lam_true = 4; data = rng.poisson(lam_true, 10); S, n_obs = int(data.sum()), len(data)
pg_priors = {"Vague Gamma(1, 0.1)": (1, .1), "Informative Gamma(8, 2)": (8, 2), "Misleading Gamma(30, 2)": (30, 2)}
pg = {"data": data.tolist(), "sum": S, "n": n_obs, "mle": S / n_obs, "post": {}}
kk = np.arange(0, 25)
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4)); lam = np.linspace(0.01, 20, 600)
for (name, (a, b)), c in zip(pg_priors.items(), COL):
    A, Bb = a + S, b + n_obs
    pm = A / Bb; lo, hi = stats.gamma.ppf([.025, .975], A, scale=1 / Bb)
    pred = stats.nbinom.pmf(kk, A, Bb / (Bb + 1))             # posterior predictive: NegBin(A, p = B/(B+1))
    p10 = stats.nbinom.sf(9, A, Bb / (Bb + 1))
    pg["post"][name] = {"mean": pm, "lo": lo, "hi": hi, "p_ge10": float(p10), "prior_mean": a / b}
    axs[0].plot(lam, stats.gamma.pdf(lam, A, scale=1 / Bb), color=c, label=name); axs[0].plot(lam, stats.gamma.pdf(lam, a, scale=1 / b), color=c, ls=":", lw=1)
    axs[1].plot(kk, pred, "o-", ms=3, color=c, label=name)
plug = stats.poisson.pmf(kk, S / n_obs); pg["plugin_p_ge10"] = float(stats.poisson.sf(9, S / n_obs))
axs[1].plot(kk, plug, "s--", ms=3, color=TXT, label=f"plug-in Poisson({S/n_obs:.1f})")
axs[0].axvline(lam_true, color=TXT, lw=.8); axs[0].set_title("prior (dotted) and posterior of λ  (true λ = 4, vertical line)"); axs[0].set_xlabel("λ"); axs[0].legend(fontsize=8)
axs[1].set_title("posterior predictive for tomorrow’s count"); axs[1].set_xlabel("count"); axs[1].legend(fontsize=8)
R["pg"] = pg; save(fig, "hw8_poisson.png")

# ---- 2d frequentist coverage of credible intervals (exact, n = 20)
n = 20; kv = np.arange(n + 1); pgrid = np.linspace(0.01, .99, 491)
def intervals(a, b): return stats.beta.ppf(.025, a + kv, b + n - kv), stats.beta.ppf(.975, a + kv, b + n - kv)
ints = {"Uniform Beta(1,1)": intervals(1, 1), "Jeffreys Beta(½,½)": intervals(.5, .5), "Misleading Beta(2,20)": intervals(2, 20)}
ph = kv / n; se = np.sqrt(ph * (1 - ph) / n); ints["Wald (frequentist)"] = (ph - 1.96 * se, ph + 1.96 * se)
ints["Clopper–Pearson"] = (np.where(kv > 0, stats.beta.ppf(.025, np.maximum(kv, 1e-9), n - kv + 1), 0.0), np.where(kv < n, stats.beta.ppf(.975, kv + 1, np.maximum(n - kv, 1e-9)), 1.0))
cov = {}
pm_ = stats.binom.pmf(kv[None, :], n, pgrid[:, None])
for name, (lo, hi) in ints.items():
    ok = (lo[None, :] <= pgrid[:, None]) & (pgrid[:, None] <= hi[None, :]); cov[name] = (pm_ * ok).sum(1)
R["cov"] = {name: {"mean": float(v[(pgrid >= .05) & (pgrid <= .95)].mean()), "min": float(v[(pgrid >= .05) & (pgrid <= .95)].min()), "at_0.7": float(v[np.argmin(abs(pgrid - .7))]), "at_0.1": float(v[np.argmin(abs(pgrid - .1))])} for name, v in cov.items()}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.4))
for (name, v), c in zip(cov.items(), COL + [COL[0]]): ax.plot(pgrid, v, color=c, lw=1.2, label=name)
ax.axhline(.95, color=TXT, ls="--", lw=1); ax.set_ylim(.6, 1.01); ax.set_xlabel("true p"); ax.set_ylabel("frequentist coverage"); ax.set_title("Exact coverage of nominal 95% intervals, n = 20"); ax.legend(fontsize=8, ncol=2, loc="lower center")
save(fig, "hw8_coverage.png")
